newsitem.title: UK: Sterling bulls poised to test UK govt's resolve.
newsitem.headline: Sterling bulls poised to test UK govt's resolve.

text.p: UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown on Thursday fired a shot across the bows of currency traders who have propelled sterling to its highest level in six years, but analysts said he is likely to have a battle on his hands.
Brown publicly protested against the pound's double-digit relentless surge this year against the currencies of Britain's main trading partners, a move which is beginning to distress UK exporters.
Sterling bulls took heed but are not about to back off without a fight from what has been effectively a one-way bet for the past year.

Economists said Brown passed up the opportunity to use his maiden budget speech on Wednesday to curb domestic demand. That leaves interest-rate policy to bear the brunt of fighting inflation in the coming months.

"Intervention, verbal or otherwise, may have a short term impact but in the long-term it is the interest rate differential that everyone is focusing on," said Juergen Lindemann, senior trader at IBJ. Against this backdrop, "2.95 marks is the next hurdle for sterling and three is the target."

Sterling was at 2.9397/07 marks at 1230 GMT from the five-year high of 2.9430 it vaulted to late Wednesday after the budget. Cable was last at $1.6765/70 from the five-month high of $1.6785 it set yesterday.
The pound's trade-weighted index is at 103.3, the strongest it has been since January 29, 1991.
Verbal intervention usually reaps diminishing returns, analysts said, particularly when it is trying to work against fundamentals like interest rate differentials.
That could force the UK monetary authorities to intervene to sell sterling on the open markets and boost its foreign exchange reserves from current levels of about $40 billion.
This will make a bigger dent in sterling bullishness, but exporters aren't holding out great hopes of it working for long.

"I can see sterling going to three against the mark and 10 to the French franc and it is absolutely disastrous," said Derek Westcott, the sales and managing director at Cash Bases, a Newhaven-based company which designs and makes cash boxes, mainly for overseas markets.

Renewing sterling's membership of the European Union's exchange rate mechanism (ERM), blamed by many for prolonging the UK recession in the early 1990s, could be one way of puncturing the pound's rally, some analysts said.

Money which has flowed into sterling on the view that it is a safe haven from concern about the European single currency will leave again if Britain signals it wants closer integration with continental Europe.
"The UK cannot afford to be outside EMU for long and all the alarm bells will start ringing if sterling goes above three marks," said Lindemann at IBJ.
Sterling is also ultimately seen falling victim to its own success.
Slumping exports and the imports sucked in as a result of the British consumers' increased purchasing power overseas will eventually feed through into a widening trade deficit and weaken the pound.
Brown "may well be more active about trying to prevent sterling from going through three marks," said Sean Shepley, international economist at CS First Boston told Reuters Financial Television.
"It may be through verbal intervention, it may be actual intervention, it may be by starting to float the idea of ERM re-entry at a (lower) central rate."
Still, "the market dynamics are going to be to go and test the authorities' resolve."
